title: Writing tests that catch bugs
summary: Write your own checks, Dojo style, and prove they catch broken implementations.

steps.title: What a good test looks like
body: The checks you have been passing all along look like this:
Each one follows **Arrange, Act, Assert**: set up inputs, call the code once, compare to an expected value. Good tests:
- have a **name that says the rule** ("zero people is refused"), so a failure explains itself
- include **edge cases**: zero, one, empty, the boundary value, the value just past it
- are **deterministic**: no real clock, no unseeded random, no shared state

steps.prompt: A discount applies to orders of **100 or more**. Which set of test inputs is best?
steps.explain: Bugs live at boundaries: `>` vs `>=` is caught only by testing exactly 100, and 99 proves the other side.

steps.title: Tests are code that catches bugs
body: How do you know a test is any good? Break the code on purpose and see whether the test notices. This is **mutation testing**: if a deliberately wrong implementation still passes, your tests have a gap.
In the next steps you write the tests. Each test is a method that receives an implementation and returns the names of checks that failed:
void Expect(string name, bool ok) { if (!ok) failed.Add(name); }
The checker runs your tests against a correct version (nothing may fail) and against broken versions (something must fail).

steps.prompt: This test suite has a gap. How many of the two broken versions does it catch?
code: void Expect(string name, bool ok) { if (!ok) failed.Add(name); }
var caught = new[] { brokenA, brokenB }.Count(b => TestIsLeap(b).Count > 0);
steps.explain: Neither is caught. `2023` and `2024` cannot tell these apart from the real rule. A test for 1900 (not leap) and 2000 (leap), and 2022 against `% 2`, would catch them.

steps.prompt: Match each check to the bug it catches in `IsLeap`.

steps.title: Catch the leap-year bugs
prompt: Write `List<string> TestIsLeap(Func<int, bool> isLeap)` with enough `Expect` checks that:
- the **correct** rule passes: divisible by 4, except centuries, except every 400 years
- every broken version the checker tries **fails at least one** check (it tries `% 4` only, ignoring the 400 rule, `% 2`, and an off-by-one on the year)
Use the `Expect` helper shown in the starter.
starter: void Expect(string name, bool ok) { if (!ok) failed.Add(name); }
solution: void Expect(string name, bool ok) { if (!ok) failed.Add(name); }
template: Func<int, bool> dojoRight = y => y % 4 == 0 && (y % 100 != 0 || y % 400 == 0);
Dojo.Eq("the correct rule passes all your checks", new List<string>(), TestIsLeap(dojoRight));
Dojo.Check("catches: divisible by 4 only", TestIsLeap(y => y % 4 == 0).Count > 0, "a version without the century rule passed");
Dojo.Check("catches: no 400-year rule", TestIsLeap(y => y % 4 == 0 && y % 100 != 0).Count > 0, "a version without the 400 rule passed");
Dojo.Check("catches: divisible by 2", TestIsLeap(y => y % 2 == 0).Count > 0, "a version using % 2 passed");
Dojo.Check("catches: off by one", TestIsLeap(y => dojoRight(y + 1)).Count > 0, "an off-by-one version passed");
hints: Think about which years distinguish each broken version from the real rule.
Add checks for 1900 (not leap), 2000 (leap) and 2022 (not leap).

steps.title: Test the boundaries
prompt: `Shipping(decimal total)` should cost 4.99 below 50, 0 from 50 upward, and throw `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` for a negative total.

Write `List<string> TestShipping(Func<decimal, decimal> shipping)` that passes for a correct implementation and catches broken ones (the checker tries `>` instead of `>=`, a missing negative check, and a wrong price).
To check for an exception, use the `Throws` helper in the starter.
starter: void Expect(string name, bool ok) { if (!ok) failed.Add(name); }
bool Throws(Action a) { try { a(); return false; } catch (ArgumentOutOfRangeException) { return true; } }
solution: void Expect(string name, bool ok) { if (!ok) failed.Add(name); }
bool Throws(Action a) { try { a(); return false; } catch (ArgumentOutOfRangeException) { return true; } }
template: decimal DojoGood(decimal t) => t < 0 ? throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(t)) : t >= 50 ? 0 : 4.99m;
Dojo.Eq("the correct version passes all your checks", new List<string>(), TestShipping(DojoGood));
Dojo.Check("catches: > instead of >=", TestShipping(t => t < 0 ? throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException() : t > 50 ? 0 : 4.99m).Count > 0, "a version where 50 pays shipping passed");
Dojo.Check("catches: no negative check", TestShipping(t => t >= 50 ? 0 : 4.99m).Count > 0, "a version that accepts negatives passed");
Dojo.Check("catches: wrong price", TestShipping(t => t < 0 ? throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException() : t >= 50 ? 0 : 5.99m).Count > 0, "a version charging 5.99 passed");
